title: Tries
summary: A tree of characters that makes prefix questions and autocomplete natural.
keyPoints: Each edge in a trie represents one character; a path from the root spells a prefix.
A node can mark the end of a word or store a count of words that pass through it.
Insert, search, and prefix checks cost O(L), where L is the length of the word or prefix.
Tries share prefixes, so many words can be stored with less duplication than a list of full strings.

complexity.note: At most one new node per character.
Follow the characters, then check the end marker.
Walk the prefix, then enumerate below it.

commonMistakes: Confusing a prefix match with a full-word match and forgetting the end-of-word marker.
Storing whole strings at every node instead of sharing one path per prefix.
Using a trie when a hash set of whole strings is enough; prefixes are the reason to choose a trie.
Forgetting that an empty prefix matches every stored word.
interviewNotes: Say what each node stores: children, an end marker, and optionally a count or list of suggestions.
If the alphabet is fixed and small, an array of children can be faster than a hash map.
For autocomplete, combine the trie with a top-k list at each node or a ranking score.

checkYourself.question: Why is inserting a word O(L) rather than O(n) for n words?
checkYourself.answer: The work depends on the length of the word being inserted, not on how many other words are already stored.

checkYourself.question: What does a node's count mean in Prefix Ledger?
checkYourself.answer: The number of inserted words whose path passed through that node, which equals the number of words with that prefix.

checkYourself.question: When is a trie a better choice than a hash set?
checkYourself.answer: When the questions are about prefixes, shared beginnings, or ordered suggestions rather than exact membership.
